paragraphs: A symmetric function gives the same answer regardless of the order of its inputs. Neural networks can enforce this property, but guarantees for sets of a fixed size do not automatically explain what happens when the number of inputs changes. This paper studies that broader kind of generalization, which matters for applications involving point clouds or collections of particles.

The authors treat sets through probability measures, allowing functions on differently sized collections to be studied within a shared mathematical framework. They focus on shallow neural architectures and establish bounds on both approximation and generalization. Different regularization choices, including RKHS and variation norms, lead to a hierarchy of function spaces with different degrees of nonlinear learning.

The resulting models can be learned efficiently and have generalization guarantees that extend across input sizes. Empirical results support this behavior. The contribution is a framework connecting representation, regularization, and learning across collection sizes, extending the analysis beyond whether a network respects input order.
icml-2021-a-functional-perspective-on-le.tldr: Viewing unordered collections as probability measures yields neural models with learning guarantees that extend across input sizes.

paragraphs: Asynchronous training lets parts of a convolutional neural network learn without waiting for every other part. This creates a problem called gradient staleness: an update can reflect an earlier state of the network. The paper identifies this as a major source of trouble in decoupled learning, where ignoring stale gradients can weaken generalization or even cause training to diverge.

The proposed accumulated decoupled learning method collects gradients within individual modules to mitigate this staleness. The authors also define a quantitative measure of staleness, making its reduction something that can be tracked and visualized. Their theoretical analysis establishes convergence to critical points despite the asynchronous learning process; this is a convergence result, rather than a guarantee of finding the best possible solution.

Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet show promising generalization while compared methods suffer reduced generalization or divergence. ADL also trains fastest among the methods compared. Together, these results support gradient accumulation as a way to retain asynchronous training speed while addressing a specific source of instability.
icml-2021-accumulated-decoupled-learning.tldr: Accumulating gradients within network modules mitigates stale updates and supports fast, convergent asynchronous training.

paragraphs: A neural network can make useful predictions while expressing unreliable confidence, especially when its inputs differ from the training distribution. This paper introduces amortized conditional normalized maximum likelihood, or ACNML, to improve uncertainty estimation and calibration under such shifts. The aim is a scalable approach that can work with deep networks across different tasks.

The method starts from conditional normalized maximum likelihood, a coding scheme with minimax optimal properties under the minimum description length principle. Its obstacle is computational: exact evaluation is intractable for all but simple model classes. ACNML uses approximate Bayesian inference to construct a tractable approximation to the distribution defined by that scheme.

The approach can use any approximate inference algorithm that supplies tractable posterior densities over model parameters. This requirement makes the method broadly compatible while specifying what its inference component must provide. Experiments find favorable calibration compared with several previous uncertainty methods under distribution shift. These results support the practical approximation without establishing that it inherits every optimality property of exact CNML.
icml-2021-amortized-conditional-normaliz.tldr: ACNML approximates a theoretically grounded predictive distribution to improve neural-network calibration under distribution shift.

paragraphs: Incorrect training labels can push a neural network toward the wrong predictions, making the choice of training loss especially important. Symmetric loss functions offer robustness to label noise, but the symmetry requirement restricts which losses can be used. This paper introduces asymmetric loss functions as a broader class for learning with arbitrary types of label noise.

The authors study how these losses connect to classification quality through classification calibration, excess risk bounds, and noise tolerance. These properties address whether optimizing a loss supports good classification and how errors in that optimization relate to prediction errors. They also define an asymmetry ratio that measures a loss function's asymmetry and establish necessary and sufficient conditions for modified versions of several common losses to belong to the class.

Empirically, larger asymmetry ratios are associated with better robustness. Benchmark experiments also show that asymmetric losses can outperform previous leading methods. The contribution therefore combines a theoretical loss-design framework with evidence that its measurable properties can help guide practical learning from unreliable labels.
icml-2021-asymmetric-loss-functions-for-.tldr: Asymmetric losses broaden the design of noise-robust training objectives and can outperform existing methods on noisy-label benchmarks.

paragraphs: Many methods for learning from incorrect labels need a transition matrix describing how labels become corrupted. Estimating this matrix often depends on anchor points: examples whose true class is almost certain. Such examples can be difficult to identify, and having too few of them can limit estimation accuracy even when the surrounding dataset is large.

This paper replaces reliance on anchor points with a clusterability condition on feature representations. The method examines agreement among noisy labels attached to nearby representations. The authors prove that, with clusterable representations, agreement information involving up to three neighboring labels is sufficient to identify a unique transition matrix.

This matters because the estimator can use substantially more examples than approaches restricted to anchor points, yielding better sample complexity. Experiments assess its estimates using synthetic label noise on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, plus human labeling errors on Clothing1M and a collected CIFAR-10 annotation set. The findings support clusterability as a useful alternative assumption for estimating label corruption, with accuracy benefits demonstrated across both synthetic and human noise.
icml-2021-clusterability-as-an-alternati.tldr: Under a clusterability condition, neighboring noisy-label agreements suffice to estimate label corruption without relying on anchor points.

paragraphs: Disentanglement learning seeks representations in which separate factors of variation have distinct, structured effects. Conventional approaches often represent those changes as movement along individual coordinates in a vector space. This paper argues that this choice can create extra work: the model must discard properties of the variations, such as differences in scale or level of abstraction, to fit that structure.

The authors instead represent variations using groups, mathematical structures that describe how transformations combine. Their goal is to learn a structure that reflects changes in the data while preserving more of their properties. To make training manageable, they focus on Lie groups and parameterize them through Lie algebra, from which they derive constraints for disentanglement learning.

They implement this approach in a Commutative Lie Group VAE. Experiments show that the model can learn disentangled representations without supervision and achieve leading performance without extra constraints. The results support changing the structure of the latent representation itself as a way to improve how a model captures separate sources of variation.
icml-2021-commutative-lie-group-vae-for-.tldr: A group-based VAE learns disentangled representations using a latent structure designed to preserve properties of data variations.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning produces representations that work well across many later tasks, but explaining that success requires understanding what the representations recover. This paper studies whether a contrastive objective can uncover the process responsible for generating observed data. That perspective connects useful features to underlying generative structure rather than treating their usefulness only as an experimental outcome.

The authors prove that feedforward models trained with objectives from the InfoNCE family can implicitly invert the underlying generative model under specified statistical assumptions. In plain language, learning can recover a representation that works backward from observations toward the structure that produced them. The proof links contrastive learning with generative modeling and nonlinear independent component analysis.

Empirical results find behavior consistent with the theory even when its statistical assumptions are severely violated. That evidence suggests broader practical relevance, while the formal guarantee remains tied to its assumptions. The work offers an explanation for what contrastive representations learn and a theoretical basis from which more effective contrastive losses could be developed.
icml-2021-contrastive-learning-inverts-t.tldr: Under statistical assumptions, InfoNCE-based contrastive learning implicitly inverts the data-generating model, with empirical support beyond those assumptions.

paragraphs: Federated learning combines learning from users whose data remain local. When users differ substantially, directly averaging their model parameters can produce a drifting global model that converges slowly. Knowledge distillation offers another way to combine their knowledge, but existing approaches can require a proxy dataset and may not fully use the combined knowledge to improve local training.

This paper proposes a data-free distillation method in which the server learns a lightweight generator that brings together information from users. The generator is then sent back to users, where its learned knowledge guides local model training. This creates a path for aggregated information to influence subsequent learning on individual devices.

The approach addresses both the need for a proxy dataset and the limited use of shared knowledge in local updates. Empirical studies, supported by theoretical implications, show better generalization with fewer communication rounds than the compared leading methods. The findings suggest that exchanging a learned source of guidance can improve how heterogeneous users contribute to and benefit from federated learning.
icml-2021-data-free-knowledge-distillati.tldr: A server-trained generator shares distilled user knowledge to improve heterogeneous federated learning without requiring a proxy dataset.

paragraphs: Variational autoencoders can learn representations whose coordinates correspond to meaningful factors in data, despite theoretical arguments against unrestricted unsupervised disentanglement. This paper investigates the inductive bias behind that apparent tension. Its central finding is that, in classical datasets, variance created by the generating factors aligns conveniently with latent directions encouraged by the VAE objective.

The authors test this explanation by constructing carefully modified versions of standard datasets. The modifications preserve the generative factors perfectly while applying mild transformations to images that make small changes to variance. These changes hide the convenient correlation structure that VAE-based architectures would otherwise exploit, separating the presence of meaningful factors from the statistical arrangement that helps reveal them.

On the modified datasets, leading VAE-based disentanglement architectures fail to produce disentangled representations, while a non-variational method retains its performance. This supports the claim that favorable variance structure is pivotal to the observed VAE successes. It also shows why preserving a dataset's underlying factors does not necessarily preserve a particular model family's ability to discover them.
icml-2021-demystifying-inductive-biases-.tldr: Carefully altered datasets reveal how VAE disentanglement depends on favorable alignment between data variance and the training objective.

paragraphs: A model can achieve low training error by using correlations that happen to appear in its dataset but do not reflect the underlying prediction problem. This paper analyzes such spurious representations using minimal sufficient statistics, an information-theoretic way to describe information needed for prediction. The authors prove that even a shift affecting only the input distribution can lead models to learn spurious features.

Group distributionally robust optimization addresses distribution shift by minimizing the worst training loss across predefined groups. The paper shows that this approach can fail when the groups do not capture the spurious correlations present in the data. Protecting each group as a whole may therefore leave important patterns within those groups insufficiently addressed.

The proposed method optimizes worst-case losses over a more flexible family of distributions defined jointly over groups and individual examples. Experiments on one image task and two language tasks show significantly greater robustness than comparable baselines across different partitions. The results connect the theoretical diagnosis to a practical change in how robust optimization represents possible distribution shifts.
icml-2021-examining-and-combating-spurio.tldr: Robust optimization over both groups and individual examples helps address spurious correlations that predefined groups can miss.

paragraphs: An agent facing a new task often needs to explore before it knows how to obtain rewards. Meta-learning aims to teach this adaptation behavior across tasks, but the training process itself also needs useful exploration. Existing approaches can rely on frequent rewards during meta-training and fail severely when rewards are sparse, leaving little feedback about which behavior is productive.

HyperX addresses this problem by adding reward bonuses during meta-training. These bonuses encourage exploration in an approximate hyper-state space, where a hyper-state combines the current environment state with the agent's belief about its task. Including task belief makes the exploration target reflect both where the agent is and what it currently understands about the problem.

Experiments show that HyperX learns better task-exploration behavior and adapts more successfully to new tasks than existing methods. The contribution is an exploration mechanism for the process of learning to adapt: improving the experiences available during meta-training helps the agent acquire behavior useful when it later encounters an unfamiliar task.
icml-2021-exploration-in-approximate-hyp.tldr: HyperX rewards exploration of environment states and task beliefs during meta-training, improving adaptation to new tasks empirically.

paragraphs: Effective communication requires adapting to what a conversational partner understands. This paper studies few-shot language coordination, where an agent must quickly adjust to partners with different linguistic abilities. Training involves a population of partners, creating a setting in which the lead agent needs to communicate successfully with previously unseen agents in that population.

The approach draws on theory of mind by having the speaker explicitly model the listener's mental state. Through interaction, speakers learn to predict how their current partner will respond to different messages. These predictions inform which instructions to send, balancing the communicative goal against the costs of the messages used to achieve it.

Experiments in a referential game and a language navigation task support the benefit of explicit partner modeling. The agents learn to predict partner reactions on the fly, helping them tailor communication during short interactions. The findings also suggest that studying language acquisition as a social, goal-directed process can be useful for building agents that coordinate across differences in language ability.
icml-2021-few-shot-language-coordination.tldr: Speakers that model their listeners' reactions learn to adapt communication quickly across partners with different language abilities.

paragraphs: In some recommendation settings, a learning system cannot directly choose which option gets tried. It must offer incentives that influence users' choices. This paper adds another complication: rewarding users with particular preferences attracts more users with similar preferences, so incentives can change the population that the system will encounter in the future.

The authors formalize these effects in a multi-armed bandit model with random arm selection and self-reinforcing preferences. The agent must balance exploration and exploitation while also controlling incentive payments. Using properties of a multi-color Polya urn model with nonlinear feedback, they develop two policies called At-Least-n Explore-Then-Commit and UCB-List.

For both policies, the authors prove that expected regret and expected total payment grow only logarithmically with the time horizon. Within the proposed model, this means the cost of learning and the spending needed to influence choices remain controlled as interactions accumulate. Numerical simulations verify the policies' performance and examine robustness across settings, complementing the theoretical treatment of incentives and changing user preferences.
icml-2021-incentivized-bandit-learning-w.tldr: Two bandit policies achieve logarithmic expected regret and incentive spending in a model with self-reinforcing user preferences.

paragraphs: Cooperating agents need to consider both how well they perform together and how fairly the benefits are distributed. This paper expresses that goal through a welfare function that explicitly captures efficiency and equity. Doing so makes fairness part of the learning objective, giving the agents a mathematical criterion for balancing overall outcomes with their distribution.

The authors analyze convergence of policy-gradient learning for this objective and propose a neural architecture containing two subnetworks designed around efficiency and equity. Their experiments demonstrate the importance of both components. The framework accepts any differentiable or subdifferentiable welfare function, allowing it to accommodate different established notions of fairness, including proportional fairness and generalized Gini welfare.

The method supports centralized training with decentralized execution as well as fully decentralized learning. Experiments across several domains show that it can substantially improve both efficiency and equity over previous methods. The contribution is a general way to connect a chosen definition of social welfare to the architecture and optimization used by cooperating reinforcement-learning agents.
icml-2021-learning-fair-policies-in-dece.tldr: A welfare-based learning objective and two-part neural architecture help cooperative agents improve both efficiency and equity.

paragraphs: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo samples from complex probability distributions, but evaluating gradients using a large dataset can be expensive. Replacing full gradients with estimates from smaller data batches reduces work per iteration, while raising questions about whether sampling still approaches the intended distribution. This paper develops a framework for analyzing that convergence.

The framework applies to strongly log-concave, log-smooth target distributions. It guarantees convergence measured by 2-Wasserstein distance when the gradient estimator is unbiased and its variance stays bounded along the algorithm's trajectory. These conditions connect the quality of the gradient estimates to the behavior of the sampling process, rather than assuming that cheaper gradients automatically give an efficient sampler.

The authors analyze mini-batch stochastic gradients, SVRG, SAGA, and control variate gradients within the framework. Their theory explains inefficiency in the mini-batch approach and suggests that SVRG and SAGA suit high-precision tasks, while control variates perform better for large datasets. Experiments support these findings, showing how convergence analysis can inform the choice of stochastic gradient estimator.
icml-2021-on-the-convergence-of-hamilton.tldr: A convergence framework for stochastic-gradient HMC explains how gradient estimators affect sampling efficiency under specified distributional assumptions.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to estimate a smooth function of an unknown high-dimensional parameter when every observation is that parameter plus independent Gaussian noise. The function has an additive structure, meaning its components combine through addition. This structure provides information that can improve estimation beyond treating the target as an unrestricted smooth function.

Building on iterative bootstrap bias reduction, the authors derive an estimator that reduces systematic estimation error. They establish normal approximation results and show that the estimator can become asymptotically normal under a weaker smoothness requirement than for general smooth functions. The additive structure is what permits this relaxation, and the results also establish asymptotic efficiency.

Upper and lower bounds on mean squared error show that the estimator is minimax optimal for the smoothness class studied. Simulations support the analysis and show advantages over a plug-in approach for reducing bias and constructing confidence intervals. The work connects structural knowledge about the target function to both optimal estimation guarantees and improved uncertainty assessment.
icml-2021-optimal-estimation-of-high-dim.tldr: Exploiting additive structure enables a bias-reduced estimator with asymptotic efficiency and minimax guarantees under Gaussian observation noise.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to identify the best option from noisy observations when an adversary can corrupt some of the evidence. The learner has a fixed sampling budget and does not know the corruption amount. The proposed randomized algorithm, Probabilistic Sequential Shrinking, uses a parameter to balance identification success against how far the selected option may be from optimal.

When corruption per step stays below a threshold, the probability of finding the best option approaches one as the budget grows. Above that threshold, the quality gap degrades gracefully with corruption. The authors also prove that sufficiently large corruption prevents any algorithm from achieving identification probability approaching one, establishing a genuine boundary on what more sampling can accomplish.

Randomization is central to the protection. An attack causes high failure probability for the deterministic Successive Halving method while the proposed algorithm remains robust. Without corruption, its parameter-two setting matches Successive Halving's guarantee. Numerical experiments support the theory, including the distinction between reliable exact identification and controlled degradation.
icml-2021-probabilistic-sequential-shrin.tldr: Randomized sequential shrinking identifies the best option under limited corruption and degrades gracefully when corruption is larger.

paragraphs: Adversarial training aims to learn classifiers that withstand input perturbations, but incorrect labels complicate that goal. This paper studies linear decision boundaries, or halfspaces, with agnostic label noise. It measures performance relative to the best robust halfspace available for a specified perturbation radius, allowing the benchmark itself to have nonzero error.

For standard binary cross-entropy, the authors bound robust error by roughly the square root of that benchmark error for Euclidean perturbations. For maximum-coordinate perturbations, the bound also includes a factor of the dimension raised to one quarter. These guarantees require anti-concentration properties of the input distribution, satisfied by isotropic log-concave distributions among others.

Using a nonconvex sigmoidal loss improves the dependence from square-root to linear in the benchmark error, while retaining the dimension factor for maximum-coordinate perturbations. This makes the loss choice consequential for the provable quality of robust learning. The paper establishes that adversarial training can yield robust classifiers despite label noise within the analyzed setting, rather than requiring perfectly labeled data.
icml-2021-provable-robustness-of-adversa.tldr: Under anti-concentration assumptions, adversarial training learns noise-tolerant robust halfspaces, with stronger error guarantees from a sigmoidal loss.

paragraphs: Large state and action spaces make reinforcement learning difficult because learning separately about every possibility can be inefficient. This paper studies discounted Markov decision processes whose transition probabilities are linear functions of a predefined feature mapping. That assumption lets the learner use a lower-dimensional representation while retaining a structured model of how the environment changes.

The proposed algorithm achieves regret scaling, apart from logarithmic factors, as d times the square root of T divided by (1−γ) squared. Here d is feature dimension, T is the learning horizon, and γ is the discount factor. The guarantee does not require access to a generative model or strong assumptions such as ergodicity.

The authors also construct problems establishing a lower bound with the same dimension and time dependence but a discount-factor denominator of (1−γ) to the power 1.5. The two bounds place the algorithm near optimal, with a remaining factor of (1−γ) to the power −0.5. This identifies both the benefit of the feature representation and the remaining gap in discount-factor dependence.
icml-2021-provably-efficient-reinforceme.tldr: For discounted MDPs with linear transition features, a learning algorithm achieves regret close to a matching lower bound.

paragraphs: A cold boot attack examines remnants of computer memory shortly after power is removed. Although many bits have become corrupted, some survive at scattered locations. Encryption keys are often expanded into longer representations with fixed redundancies, so surviving pieces can contain enough related information to support recovery of the original key.

This paper combines a deep error-correcting technique with a modified SAT solver to recover AES keys from such corrupted information. A central contribution is expressing the AES key schedule as a computational graph implemented through a neural message-passing network. This gives the learning component a representation of the relationships built into key expansion, including the presence of Rijndael SBOX elements.

The reported results show a very large improvement over previous attack methods. The setting concerns reconstructing keys from damaged memory that retains structured information about them. The contribution demonstrates how neural processing of that structure, combined with a logical solving method, can improve recovery even though AES includes components designed to resist linear and differential cryptanalysis.
icml-2021-recovering-aes-keys-with-a-dee.tldr: Combining neural error correction with a modified SAT solver substantially improves reported AES key recovery from corrupted memory.

paragraphs: An adversarial image can fool a classifier while changing only a few pixels. Requiring each change to remain small makes the attack harder to construct, because the optimization must jointly control the number of altered pixels and their maximum change. This paper develops a homotopy algorithm to handle those requirements within one framework.

Each iteration optimizes an adversarial loss with an l0 sparsity penalty using a nonmonotone accelerated proximal gradient method. A further step controls changes in sparsity, and an optional post-attack step seeks to escape poor local minima. The authors also extend the framework to structured sparsity, broadening the types of sparse perturbations it can address.

Experiments examine targeted and untargeted attacks on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. In the reported average targeted setting, the method reduces perturbations by 42.91% and 75.03%, respectively, compared with leading methods at similar maximum perturbation magnitudes, while maintaining 100% attack success. These findings show that the tested networks can be vulnerable to substantially fewer small pixel changes than previous methods revealed.
icml-2021-sparse-and-imperceptible-adver.tldr: A homotopy attack jointly controls sparsity and perturbation size, achieving successful attacks with fewer altered pixels in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Large graphs often reside across multiple machines, making communication an important cost when constructing smaller approximations. This paper develops distributed algorithms that preserve selected relationships in a graph while limiting the messages exchanged. Its focus is on vertices of interest, allowing the approximation task to concentrate on the relationships that need to be retained.

One set of algorithms constructs spectral vertex sparsifiers, which closely preserve effective resistance distances among a chosen subset of vertices. The authors prove that their communication cost lies near a lower bound, with only a small gap. A second set constructs pair-wise spanners that approximate shortest-path distances for a target set of vertex pairs rather than every possible pair.

For the spanner construction, communication costs are much smaller than those of existing algorithms in the message-passing model. Experiments validate communication efficiency while retaining good approximation quality. The work therefore links selective preservation of graph structure with reduced distributed communication, supporting graph processing when both the network size and the cost of moving information matter.
icml-2021-spectral-vertex-sparsifiers-an.tldr: Distributed graph approximation algorithms preserve selected resistance or shortest-path distances with low communication costs.

paragraphs: Training a neural network on adversarial examples can improve its defenses, but protection learned from familiar attacks may transfer poorly to unfamiliar ones. This paper addresses that generalization problem by seeking features that remain stable across attacks while preserving the semantic information required for classification. The goal is to reduce the influence of attack-specific noise on the representation.

The authors introduce an adversarial feature-learning mechanism intended to separate invariant features from adversarial noise. They also add a normalization term in the encoded feature space to address bias between the types of attacks encountered during training and previously unseen types. Both components target the representation through which the classifier makes its decisions.

Empirical evaluations indicate that the method could provide better protection than previous leading approaches, especially against unseen attack types and adaptive attacks. This supports learning shared structure across attacks as a useful defense strategy. The findings concern the evaluated attacks and show improved transfer of protection, without establishing a universal guarantee against every possible adversarial perturbation.
icml-2021-towards-defending-against-adve.tldr: Learning features shared across attacks improves empirical protection, particularly against unseen and adaptive adversarial attacks.

paragraphs: An active visual tracker must keep following its target even when other objects obscure it or look confusingly similar. This paper trains a tracker through a multi-agent game designed to create such difficulties. The target and several distractors cooperate against the tracker, trying to make it lose the object it is meant to follow.

As the competing agents learn, different distracting behaviors emerge and expose weaknesses in the tracker. The authors support this training process with a reward function for distractors, a cross-modal teacher-student strategy, and a recurrent attention mechanism for the tracker. Together, these methods help turn the adversarial interactions into a learning process that improves resistance to distraction.

Experiments show successful distraction-robust tracking and generalization to unseen environments. The same game also serves as a way to test tracker robustness by generating challenging interactions. The contribution therefore gives learned distractors two roles: they provide difficult training experiences and help reveal where a tracker can still be misled during evaluation.
icml-2021-towards-distraction-robust-act.tldr: A game with cooperating distractors trains and tests visual trackers against learned behaviors that make targets difficult to follow.

paragraphs: Compressing an input can save information before inference, but the resulting distortion may change a classifier's decision. This paper studies that risk for majority-vote classifiers, whose predictions combine the votes of several component predictors. It seeks analytic guarantees describing how resilient the combined decision is to noise introduced by compression.

Starting from bounds on majority-vote prediction risk, the authors extend PAC-Bayesian analysis to quantify noise invariance. In binary classification, the bounds can be measured through differences in votes and agreement between pairs of voters. These quantities connect the stability of the final decision to the behavior of the predictors that compose it.

The paper combines these guarantees with measures of input distortion to guide compression while preserving subsequent classification. Validation shows how the bounds can inform the compression stage and expose worst-case consequences of poor reconstructions. This makes compression sensitive to the downstream classifier: the target is the minimum information needed for inference under the analysis, rather than reconstruction quality considered on its own.
icml-2022-pac-bayesian-bounds-on-rate-ef.tldr: PAC-Bayesian noise-invariance bounds guide input compression for majority-vote classifiers while accounting for possible classification changes.
